newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: SPT says Czech flood losses mount.
newsitem.headline: SPT says Czech flood losses mount.

text.p: Floods in the eastern Czech Republic have caused damage on the country's telephone network costing hundreds of millions of crowns, the fixed line monopoly SPT Telecom a.s. said on Wednesday.
In a statement, SPT said a total of nearly 67,000 telephone lines had been cut in the regions of Northern Moravia, Southern Moravia and Eastern Bohemia.
"It is the largest telecommunications catastrophe in the history of the Czech Republic," the statement quoted SPT General Director Svatoslav Novak as saying.
"At this moment we are not able to estimate exactly the extent of the damage, but I can say already that they will reach the range of hundreds of millions," Novak added.
SPT said teams were fighting to keep lines up in areas where electricity supplies have been cut.
Telecoms is one of several industries which have been hit hard by the worst flooding of the century. Total flood damages has not been estimated, but are believed to top 10 billion already.

Heavy rains since the weekend have claimed at least nine lives and forced the evacuation of tens of thousands of people. Dozens of houses have been swept away and more damage was expected as floods move further downstream.
Insurance firm Ceska Pojistovna a.s. , which has hundreds of thousands of clients in the affected region, said the disaster was unmatched in the country's modern history.
A number of companies had shut or slashed production due to flooding and power cuts.
Czech Television said steel maker Trinecke Zelezarny a.s. was cutting back production by half.
Car maker Skoda Automobilova a.s., a unit of Volkswagen AG , interrupted production of its Felicia model on Wednesday, as parts suppliers were cut off.
Tyre firm Barum Continental a.s., a unit of has shut entirely,
Road and rail transport in the area was suspended, and the state railways have said that repair costs are mounting.
Politicians have argued over whether a third emergency economic package might be necessary, after two such austerity packages where agreed in April and June to answer serious macroeconomic problems.

Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus rejected that a "third package" would be needed, but the government authorised over one billion crowns ($30.6 million) to be freed up for rescue operations, with long-term funds for rebuilding to be discussed later.
